idiom_name: compose over impl Fn, or move |x| g(f(x))
implementation_notes: Closures are anonymous functions implementing the Fn family of traits (doc.rust-lang.org), so a step is any `impl Fn(A) -> B` and composition is `move |x| g(f(x))` or a small generic helper; iterator adaptors (map, filter, then) apply the same closure shape to sequences. Standard Rust has no compose function, and because every closure has a distinct unnameable type, returning a chain means `impl Fn` for statically known compositions or `Box<dyn Fn>` when steps are collected dynamically - the same choice the standard documentation describes for returning closures. The helper is the idiomatic replacement for the classic combinator; a single inline closure stays clearer for one use.
pitfalls: impl Fn return types are opaque and unique per function: two chains built by the same compose call still have different types, so a Vec of chains needs Box<dyn Fn>.
Captures determine the trait: a step that moves a captured value out implements only FnOnce and cannot back a reusable chain.
Closures capturing references must outlive the chain; a compose helper returning impl Fn plus 'static bounds forces move captures and ownership transfer at the call site.

variants.name: Async composition with futures and .await
variants.idiom_name: async move block sequencing awaits; Future combinators
variants.implementation_notes: When steps await, composition happens over futures instead of values: an `async move` block sequences the awaits directly, and futures-crate combinators (map, then, and_then) compose futures as values (std::future::Future documents the model). The closure-compose helper no longer applies unchanged because each step returns a Future rather than its output, so the chain either lives inside one async block or is expressed with combinators; choose this variant when the transformation chain includes I/O and the single-threaded async shape should be preserved, and keep the synchronous variant for pure steps.
pitfalls: Futures are lazy: composing them without awaiting or spawning does nothing, and dropping the future cancels the chain silently.
Each async block has its own unnameable future type, so a stored chain of them must be boxed (BoxFuture) or wrapped in a generic struct.
Holding a non-Send value across an await makes the future non-Send and breaks multi-threaded executors; scope such values before the await.
